768.stem:
The graph of the function $f(x)=x^2$ is dilated vertically by a factor of $q^2$ and then

translated 81 units down, the transformed function is given as

$$g(x)=q^2x^2-81$$

parts.latex: When the transformed function $g(x)$ is translated $p$ units to the left, the resulting function is denoted as $h(x)$. Write an expression for $h(x)$.
Find all possible values of $p$ and $q$ if $h(x)=9x^2+36x-45$.

solutions.latex:
Translating $p$ units to the left replaces $x$ with $x+p$:
$$h(x)=q^2(x+p)^2-81$$

Equate $h(x)$ from (a) and (b):
$$\begin{aligned} q^2(x+p)^2-81&=9x^2+36x-45\\ q^2(x+p)^2&=9x^2+36x-45+81\\ q^2(x+p)^2&=9x^2+36x+36\\ q^2(x+p)^2&=9(x^2+4x+4)\\ q^2(x+p)^2&=9(x+2)^2\end{aligned}$$
Comparing both sides:
$$\begin{aligned} q^2&=9 & x+p&=x+2\\ q&=\pm3 & p&=2\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the value of $p$ or $q$, or equivalent merit
Equates the two expressions for $h(x)$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
For two functions $g(x)$ and $h(x)$, it is known that for all $a>0$, $g(a)>h(a)$.

It is also known that $h'(x)<0$ and $g'(x)>0$ for $x>0$.

How many solutions are there to $g(x)-h(x)=0$ in the domain $a>0$?

solutions.latex:
Let $d(x)=g(x)-h(x)$. Then $d'(x)=g'(x)-h'(x)$.

For $x>0$, $g'(x)>0$ and $h'(x)<0$, so $d'(x)>0$.

Also $g(a)>h(a)$ for all $a>0$, so $d(x)>0$ for every $x>0$.

Hence $g(x)-h(x)=0$ has no solution in $x>0$ (the difference never reaches $0$).

parts.latex: Find the other $x$-intercept.
Find $a$, $b$ and $c$

solutions.latex:
The parabola passes through $(0,0)$ with vertex $(3,1)$, which lies above the origin, so it is concave down.

The axis of symmetry is $x=3$, so the other $x$-intercept is the reflection of $x=0$:
$$\therefore\ x = 6$$

The zeros are $x=0$ and $x=6$, so $y=a(x-0)(x-6)=ax(x-6)$.

The point $(3,1)$ satisfies the equation:
$$\begin{aligned} 1 &= 3a(-3) \\ 1 &= -9a \\ a &= -\dfrac{1}{9}\end{aligned}$$

solutions.latex:
The factors $(x-2)^2$ and $(x+2)^2$ are never negative.

So the sign of $x(x-2)^2(x+2)^2$ is the sign of $x$, except where a squared factor is zero.

$$\begin{aligned} x(x-2)^2(x+2)^2 &> 0 &&\text{for } x>0, x\neq 2\\ x(x-2)^2(x+2)^2 &= 0 &&\text{for } x=-2,\ 0,\ 2\\ x(x-2)^2(x+2)^2 &< 0 &&\text{for } x<0, x\neq -2 \end{aligned}$$

Hence the expression is $\ge 0$ for $x\ge 0$ and at $x=-2$.

This is option A.

solutions.latex:
Solutions of $-e^x(x+1)=x^2-1$ are the intersections of $y=-e^x(x+1)$ with the parabola $y=x^2-1$.

Both pass through $(-1,0)$ and $(0,-1)$, since $x^2-1=0$ at $x=-1$ and $x^2-1=-1$ at $x=0$.

So $x=-1$ and $x=0$ are solutions. We check there are no others by comparing the two sides on each interval.

For $x>0$: $e^x\ge 1+x$, so $-e^x(x+1)\le-(x+1)^2$, and
$$-(x+1)^2-(x^2-1)=-2x(x+1)<0$$
so the exponential curve is below the parabola: no solution.

For $x<-1$: put $t=-x>1$. The equation $e^{-t}(t-1)=(t-1)(t+1)$ needs $e^{-t}=t+1$, impossible since $e^{-t}<1<t+1$: no solution.

For $-1<x<0$: divide by $x+1>0$ to get $-e^x=x-1$, that is $e^x+x-1=0$. The function $e^x+x-1$ is increasing and equals $0$ only at $x=0$, so there is no solution in this interval.

Therefore there are exactly $2$ solutions, option B.
